description: Hi everyone! We're Alex, Amina, and Dávid, three Computer Science students and space enthusiasts from Hungary. We are excited to work with real NASA data and explore something new!
summary: We built Ultracool Browser to make exploring infrared sky data easier for everyone. Search for an object by name or coordinates, and you can flip through 16 years of WISE observations, overlay data from SPHEREx, and watch objects move across the sky. The app also lets you study their movement, brightness changes, and spectra, all in one place. There are four ways to use it: Learn has short lessons and quizzes, Explore answers questions in plain language, Research offers detailed measurements and tools, and Discover scans regions of the sky for moving objects that could be worth investigating. We also tested it on real brown dwarf candidates, including WISE J231728.42-665959.3, which we classified as a mid-T dwarf (T5–T6) using its SPHEREx spectrum. Our goal was to bring together tools and datasets that would otherwise require quite a bit of manual work, making them useful for both researchers and people who are simply curious about space.
details:
What it does

Ultracool Browser brings together infrared data from WISE and SPHEREx so you can explore the same region of the sky using observations from different missions.

You can search for an object by name or coordinates. The app then retrieves images from NASA's IRSA archive, aligns observations taken between 2010 and 2026, and displays them as a flipbook. This makes it possible to see objects moving across the sky over time, with a marker showing their expected position in each image.

Besides showing the images, the app can measure an object's movement, infrared color, and brightness changes. It also compares SPHEREx spectra against 47 published brown dwarf templates to estimate their spectral types. Because SPHEREx spectra have relatively low resolution, we report a range of possible types rather than a single exact match.

These tools aren't limited to the object you originally searched for. You can click on other sources in the images and analyze those too.

Exploring the data

We made four different modes depending on what you want to do:

  • Learn: Seven short lessons with quizzes, using real examples like Barnard's Star, asteroids, and even camera artifacts.
  • Explore: For anyone who wants to understand what they're seeing. For example, if you select an object and wish to know if it's moving or not, you can get an explanation without needing to know the technical details.
  • Research: More detailed data, including measurements, uncertainties, catalogue overlays, individual exposures, and CSV exports.
  • Discover: Scans a 15-arcminute area of the sky for moving objects, filters out likely artifacts, and checks existing catalogues. Users can then review the remaining candidates and mark which ones seem real.

What we found

We didn't want to build something that only worked on a few hand-picked examples, so we tested it using real brown dwarf candidates and objects with known classifications.

One interesting case was WISE J231728.42-665959.3. It had previously been listed as a probable T6 brown dwarf based on its brightness, but hadn't received a spectrum-based classification. Comparing its SPHEREx spectrum with known templates, we found that it best matches a mid-T dwarf, around T5–T6. We also estimated its distance at roughly 30 parsecs and measured a motion of about 0.5 arcseconds per year. Interestingly, its movement doesn't match that of a nearby pair of stars, making it unlikely to be their companion.

We also checked how reliable our spectral classification was. Out of 26 known brown dwarfs, the app classified 21 within two spectral subtypes of their published types.

Discover mode was another useful test. We investigated seven objects flagged as possible new brown dwarfs, but all turned out to be either image artifacts or already known sources. It showed us how important it is to check automated detections instead of assuming every moving point is a discovery.

Why we built it

Brown dwarfs are difficult to find because they're faint and don't emit much visible light. Some of the Sun's nearest neighbors could still be undiscovered objects of this kind.

Infrared observations help, especially when we compare images taken years apart and look for movement. The problem is that these observations come from different missions, with different formats and tools needed to work with them.

We wanted to bring that process into one place. Instead of writing scripts and manually downloading and aligning images every time, users can search for a region of the sky and start exploring it directly.

The idea wasn't to automate the entire research process or replace astronomers. We wanted to make the data easier to work with, while leaving the actual interpretation to the people using it.

How we built it

We used Python and FastAPI for the backend, with Astropy, astroquery, photutils, reproject, NumPy, SciPy, and s3fs for retrieving and processing astronomical data.

The frontend is built with React, TypeScript, Vite, and Tailwind. Plotly.js handles interactive plots, while Aladin Lite provides the sky viewer and catalogue overlays.

The app runs with Docker Compose and nginx on a server with only 4 CPUs and 8 GB of RAM. To keep it usable on limited hardware, we cache processed sky regions so they don't need to be downloaded and processed again for every visit. We also added rate limiting to avoid sending too many requests to NASA's archives.
